item.title: Anisha Baid
item.description: Anisha Baid is an artist and writer based in Bangalore. Through performances, guided meditations and static objects, her work attempts to poke at the flat-scapes of the computer screen to decode computer labour through the interface - a technological tool that has converted most spaces of work into image space. Her work has been shown in international solo exhibitions including at Pittsburgh Cultural Trust, as well as at Technical Collections, Dresden (2020), GIBCA, Goteborg, Sweden and Landskrona Foto Museum, Sweden. She has been supported by various grants and awards including from the Frank Ratchye Studio for Creative Inquiry, Inlaks Foundation, the India Foundation for the Arts, the Goethe Institut, as well as the Arts and Humanities Research Council, and Bluecoat in the UK.

item.title: Black Box
item.description:
Black Box is a video game that critically explores the hidden labor underpinning AI ‘assistance’ in contemporary technology. The game re-imagines the inside of the computer - the black box - not as aflatscape but as a three dimensional landscape, where the player moves around, in the role of an ‘AI agent’. The game moves between embedded ‘mini games’ where the player performs data sorting tasks, and a more liminal space inside the computer where the landscape learns and invites players’ reflections. Emphasizing the blurred lines between ‘human’ and ‘artificial’ intelligence in this paradigm, the game opens up the subjective position of an AI assistant and invites you to reflect on what makes the work you do human.

item.title: The Data is Being Trained
item.description:
Based on online conversations between January-February 2026, this zine gathers the folklore of a new occupation: data work. It gathersoffshore workers in Hyderabad and Pune to talk about their jokes,sayings, routines, and small acts that make algorithmic labour livable and contestable. A second strand documents a nonprofit effort where volunteers and activists trained a gender-based hate speech detection model in Indian English, Tamil, and Hindi. Together, theypush questions beyond the page for all of us: What kinds of life does this infrastructure produce? The design draws on the texture of ahate speech dataset collected between 2021-2023 as well as emergent folklore of Indian IT workers on Instagram. It plays with noise, signal and interference, and answers remain for the reader to piece together.

Data is being annotated

Cheshta Arora I read the proposal before this call, and I realised that the Uli project was the main thing that we sold during the application, but then we completely turned it upside down, and we made industry data workers the centre of the zine and the Uli part just became one box in the corner of the page.

item.title: Debarun Sarkar, Cheshta Arora, Gabriele de Seta, and Luke Drozd
item.description:

item.title: My Home is a Data Workplace
item.description:
Instant Infrastructures unpacks the invisible data architectures that operate behind a single ten-minute delivery order. It traces how disparate apparatuses—from residential access controls to state policing systems—converge to track, quantify, and discipline the bodies of gig workers as they navigate the city. Visualising this extraction within the platform economy, the work-mapping apparatuses are displaced not just spatially but across an asymmetric technical chain. Within this network, value is strip-mined by an array of stakeholders: the consumer, the platform, advertising agencies, the state and AI giants. The project presents an annotated essay and a 3D spatio-infrastructural mapping,; the project exposinges the data flows that operationalise the convenience of an “instant delivery" as surveillance and control.

Ramblings: What is data work?

When I started working on this project, I had been fresh out of research on platform work in India, where my work looked at how gamification, standardisation and surveillance impact domestic workers and how it relates to larger social hierarchies. I was and am largely unfamiliar with the framing of data work.

item.title: Yatharth
item.description: Yatharth is a researcher, designer and artist based in Bengaluru, India. His research practice explores caste on digital platforms and design injustice in digital technologies. Yatharth has worked with various nonprofits, research institutes, design schools and studios in the roles of media educator, qualitative researcher, curator, creative coder and designer.

item.title: About the Project
item.description:
The digital economy has reconfigured relationships between technology and labour. Workers involved in the production and maintenance of the digital economy are subjected to intensifying exploitative social dynamics of caste, class and gender and experience new forms of precarity and inequality.

The challenge of the grant is to support the development of aesthetic modes that engage and respond to these conditions. The grantee projects bridge artistic research and academic inquiry towards new formations of evidence, critique and action.
